gap.reason: The introduction motivates the need to design and fabricate W–Cu composites with homogeneous microstructures, defect-free interfaces, and preserved thermal conductivity, overcoming a material performance limitation.

source_text:
Metal‐matrix composites (MMCs) have garnered extensive research attention due to their unique combinations of properties that are unattainable with conventional materials. Among these, W‐Cu composites stand out as one of the most successful MMC systems, widely utilized for both mechanical and functional applications. These composites achieve enhanced strength and ductility by incorporating high strength but low toughness W particles, either as a dispersed second phase or interconnected ligaments, within a ductile but low strength Cu matrix, enabling their use in a variety of fields. Furthermore, the high thermal conductivities (κ) of Cu (386 W m−1·K−1) and W (173 W m−1·K−1) make these composites particularly suitable for applications requiring efficient heat dissipation, such as heat sinks leading to a combined thermal conductivity of as high as 238 W (m K)−1 with 30% copper. Owing to these properties, W‐Cu composites are also employed in semiconductor packaging materials, where they facilitate rapid heat dissipation from electronic devices while maintaining mechanical durability. Additionally, they are used in high‐voltage electrodes, which demand a combination of high strength and electrical conductivity. Of particular note, these composites are considered promising candidates for use as joint materials in the diverters of fusion reactors. In such applications, the bonding between plasma‐facing materials (PFM) often envisioned as W based materials and Cu‐based alloys (e.g., CuCrZr) used in cooling pipes requires not only high κ but also exceptional resistance to irradiation. Especially the low sputter yield, high melting temperature, and relatively low neutron activation make W and its alloys good plasm facing materials. Of course, enhancing thermal conductivity by adding Cu fosters an even better performance.

However, producing W‐Cu composites with a homogeneous microstructure remains a significant challenge. Due to the large positive enthalpy of mixing (ΔHmix: +22 kJ mol−1) between W and Cu, these metals are not only difficult to alloy in the solid state but also tend to undergo phase separation even in the liquid state. Moreover, the substantial difference in their melting and boiling points—W (≈3422 °C) has a melting point ≈1000 °C higher than the boiling point of Cu (≈2562 °C)—renders it impractical to create a uniform microstructure through conventional casting techniques such as induction melting or arc plasma melting. (Further details on the separation behavior are provided in Figure S1, Supporting Information) Even when a composite structure is successfully formed, numerous interfacial defects, such as voids, are likely to develop between the separated phases, which can lead to reduced κ. Addressing the bonding issues between these phases is, therefore, a critical challenge.

To overcome these difficulties, various fabrication methods have been explored. One of the simplest approaches, as shown in Figure 1a, is to first prepare a W skeleton and then either pour Cu melt into the gaps or fill them with Cu powder and heat the assembly to form a composite structure. However, since this method solidifies liquid Cu within solid W precursor, achieving a defect‐free interface between the two phases can be challenging. Another approach involves using powders of both materials. As illustrated in Figure 1b,c, a composite containing coexisting phases can be created either by spark plasma sintering the W and Cu powders, or by mechanical alloying, applying severe plastic deformation. While this approach can yield finer and more homogeneous microstructures, defects such as voids can still easily form at the interfaces. To address these issues, sintering core‐shell structured alloy powders—produced by coating W particles with Cu vapor—have emerged as one of the most promising approaches for creating defect‐free W‐Cu composites, despite the complexity of the process. This method ensures near‐perfect contact between the phases, effectively minimizing heat loss during thermal transfer—a significant advantage for high‐performance applications. Moreover, the use of metal 3D printing technologies has recently gained attention as another alternative for fabricating these composites.

Schematic diagrams of various existing methods for fabricating W‐Cu composites: a) Cu melt infiltration into a W skeleton, b) spark plasma sintering of W and Cu powders, c) mechanical alloying, and (d) 3D printing.

The Liquid Metal Dealloying (LMD) process, introduced by Wada et al., has emerged as a groundbreaking technique for fabricating MMCs that are challenging to produce using conventional methods. In this process, a precursor binary alloy is exposed to the liquid phase of a third metal. The liquid dissolves one element (reactive with the liquid) from the precursor and infiltrates the binary alloy leaving a defect‐free interface between the infiltrated element and one of the precursor elements (non‐reactive). Leveraging this method, McCue et al. successfully synthesized Ta‐Cu composites by reacting Ta‐Ti alloy precursors with Cu melts. Building on this innovative approach, the present study employs the LMD process to fabricate composite materials comprising an irradiation‐resistant W‐rich refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) and Cu.

queries.broad: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: W and Cu have a positive enthalpy of mixing of +22 kJ mol−1 and strongly mismatched thermal limits: W melts near 3422 °C, roughly 1000 °C above the boiling point of Cu near 2562 °C. Consequently, conventional melting cannot readily produce a homogeneous W–Cu composite, and phase separation and interfacial voids can reduce thermal conductivity. Cu-melt or Cu-powder filling of a W skeleton can leave defective interfaces; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can refine and homogenize the structure but still permit interfacial voids; coating W particles with Cu vapor before sintering can provide near-perfect contact but is complex; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Subject to the requirements of high thermal conductivity, mechanical durability, and irradiation resistance for fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could produce a more homogeneous W–Cu composite with better bonded, lower-defect interfaces than these baselines? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to a named existing baseline, the processing and operating conditions over which it should remain valid, the prior evidence supporting it, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

queries.expert_context: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.
